1151070394753110_122116049787342312.caption: At the height of his literary fame, Oscar Wilde was convicted of 'gross indecency' in 1895 and sentenced to two years of hard labor, which broke his physical health.  During his imprisonment, his wife Constance fled the country with their two sons, changing their last names to Holland to escape the public scandal. Wilde was stripped of his parental rights.  After his release, Wilde was exiled to France, where he lived in poverty and declining health. He died in a cheap Paris hotel room at age 46, having never seen his children again.  Source: Oscar Wilde trial transcripts, letters from Constance Wilde.  #OscarWilde #HiddenHistory #LiteraryHistory #TrueHistory

1151070394753110_122116049859342312.caption: Roald Dahl, the author of Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, faced multiple family disasters. In 1960, his infant son Theo's carriage was struck by a taxi, leaving him with brain damage and hydrocephalus.  In 1962, his oldest daughter Olivia died from measles encephalitis at age seven. Dahl was devastated and kept her photographs in his writing hut until his own death.  In 1965, while pregnant with their fifth child, his wife Patricia Neal suffered three massive brain aneurysms. Dahl personally managed her grueling rehabilitation program, helping her relearn to walk and talk.  Source: Roald Dahl biographical archives, Patricia Neal's memoirs.  #RoaldDahl #HiddenHistory #LiteraryHistory #TrueHistory

1151070394753110_122116050003342312.caption: Marie Curie's husband and scientific partner, Pierre Curie, was tragically killed in 1906 when he was run over by a heavy horse-drawn carriage in Paris, leaving Marie a widow at 38.  She carried on their research, discovering radium and polonium. Unaware of the dangers of radiation, she kept test tubes of radioactive isotopes in her pockets and drawers.  Marie died in 1934 of aplastic anemia caused by radiation exposure. Her oldest daughter, Irène Joliot-Curie, who also won a Nobel Prize for chemistry, died of leukemia in 1956 due to her own radiation exposure.  Source: Nobel Prize archives, Curie family laboratory records.  #MarieCurie #HiddenHistory #ScienceHistory #TrueHistory

1151070394753110_122116050129342312.caption: Sir Arthur Conan Doyle, creator of Sherlock Holmes, faced personal tragedies that reshaped his life. His first wife Louisa died of tuberculosis in 1906 after a long illness.  During World War I, his oldest son Kingsley was severely wounded at the Battle of the Somme and died of influenza in 1918. Shortly after, Doyle's younger brother Innes also died of pneumonia.  The grief drove Doyle, a medical doctor, to reject his rationalism. He spent his final years actively promoting spiritualism, spending vast sums of money trying to prove it was possible to communicate with the dead.  Source: Arthur Conan Doyle biographical archives, spiritualist lecture records.  #ArthurConanDoyle #HiddenHistory #SherlockHolmes #TrueHistory

1151070394753110_122116050345342312.caption: When Malcolm X was six years old, his father Earl Little died after being run over by a streetcar in Michigan — an incident the family strongly believed was a white supremacist murder, though officials ruled it an accident. 1151070394753110_122116043883342312.caption: In the late 1950s, Thalidomide was marketed across Europe, Canada, and dozens of countries as a "completely safe" treatment for morning sickness in pregnant women. In the US, FDA medical officer Dr. Frances Kelsey repeatedly refused to approve the drug, citing insufficient safety data — a decision credited with sparing the US from the worst of the crisis.  The disaster directly led to the 1962 Kefauver-Harris Amendment, which created the modern US drug safety and efficacy testing system still used today.  Source: FDA historical archives, Kefauver-Harris Amendment 1962. Follow.  #Thalidomide #HiddenHistory #FrancesKelsey #TrueHistory
